  How a deal is found, and why it cannot simply be looked up
  
    
    
    A deal id is a hash of the deal, not an address. It says exactly what the
    document is — change one character of the body and the id no longer matches — but it says
    nothing about where a copy lives. That is the whole point: a deal is verifiable wherever
    you got it, so it needs no trusted registry. It is also the catch: from an id alone, nothing
    tells you who published it.
    

    
    So this page tries, in order:
    
    
      
      
    1. Publishers it knows. Each one publishes <base>/deals/index.json
      listing every deal it has, and <base>/deals/<id>.json for the body —
      the same files a signer vendors with
      kea/tools/catalogue.cjs vendor --from <base>. Known here:
      .
      2. 
      
    2. The pool. Anything being raised right now carries its policy with it, so a live
      deal resolves even if nobody publishes it. The pool holds about an hour, so this only finds
      deals in flight.
      3. 
      
    3. A publisher you name. Put a base URL in the second box and it is asked the same
      two questions. This is the decentralised case: you knew who to ask, so you asked them.
      4. 
    
    

    
    Every answer is checked. Whatever the source, the body is re-hashed here in your
    browser and compared to the id — JCS (RFC 8785) for a v2 policy, PHP json_encode
    form for a v1 template. A verified badge means this really is the
    deal that id names. does not match means the copy is wrong or
    altered, and you should not trust it whoever served it.
    

    
    What is not here. There is no database of v2 deals, and deliberately so — a registry
    would be a thing to trust, and the hash already does that job. A quiet deal that nobody
    publishes and nobody is raising is not findable from its id, by design. If you want a deal to
    be findable, publish it: a directory of deals/ on any web host is the entire
    protocol.
    

    
    v1 deals. The 2022–2026 archive has its own browser at
    /legacy/deals/ and its own lookup, and is being retired. This page
    is v2-first: it will read and verify a v1 template if a publisher serves one, but it does not
    search the archive. If nothing is found here, that is the other place to look.
